title: Higher Education Legislation Amendment (Student Services and Amenities, and Other Measures) Bill 2009

divisions.question: Higher Education Legislation Amendment (Student Services and Amenities, and Other Measures) Bill 2009 - Second Reading - Read a second time

The majority voted against an [amendment](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2009-08-17.91.1) introduced by Senator [Sarah Hanson-Young](http://publicwhip-rails.openaustraliafoundation.org.au/mp.php?mpn=Sarah_Hanson-Young&mpc=Senate&house=senate), which means that it was unsuccessful. The Senator explained that the amendment "relates directly to the issues of compliance and monitoring".(Read Senator Hanson-Young's full explanation [here](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2009-08-17.91.1). ) The amendment was: _(3) Schedule 1, item 5, page 5 (after line 28), at the end of section 19-38, add:_ _Accountability of expenditure_ _(6) Each higher education provider must include in each report it prepares for the purposes of section 19-10 the following information in relation to the period covered by the report:_ _(a) details of amounts collected as student services and amenities fees during that period;_ _(b) details of the expenditure of such amounts paid to the provider._ _(7) Each higher education provider must provide a copy of that information to the department in the form approved by the Minister._ _(8) The department must publish on its website the information it receives under subsection (7)._ Background to the bill Compulsory student union fees were abolished under then Prime Minister John Howard’s Coalition Government with the [Higher Education Support Amendment (Abolition of Compulsory Upfront Student Union Fees) Bill 2005](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r2283). This meant that universities could no longer require students to pay a compulsory fee for facilities, amenities or services that were not of an academic nature. This bill aims to re-introduce a compulsory student services and amenities fee.(More information about this bill and its context can be found [here](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd0809/09bd107).) speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The speaker moved that the bills proceed without formalities, be taken together, and read a first time, and indicated that after the second reading debate is adjourned they will move to list the bills separately on the Notice Paper.

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The Higher Education Legislation Amendment Bill 2009 allows universities to charge a compulsory student services fee capped at $250 per year from July 2009, with a new SA-HELP loan scheme for eligible students, and prohibits using the fee to support political parties. The Customs Legislation Amendment Bill 2009 renames the Australian Customs Service to the Australian Customs and Border Protection Service to reflect its lead role on maritime people smuggling.

speeches.speaker: Brett Mason
speeches.brief: The coalition opposed the Higher Education Legislation Amendment (Student Services and Amenities, and Other Measures) Bill 2009, arguing that students should not be forced to pay for services they cannot or will not use, citing that 66.2% of students are mature-age and only 46.7% are full-time. The bill was criticised for failing to prevent compulsory student fees from being spent on political causes and for lacking effective enforcement mechanisms.

speeches.speaker: Mitch Fifield
speeches.brief: The debate centred on the Higher Education Legislation Amendment (Student Services and Amenities, and Other Measures) Bill 2009, which would impose a compulsory student services fee of up to $250 per year. Opponents argued it broke a pre-election promise and reintroduced compulsory student unionism, while supporters said it was needed to restore student services after the previous government's voluntary student unionism cuts.

speeches.speaker: Michaelia Cash
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the bill imposes a compulsory $250 student services fee, breaking Labor’s 2007 election promise, and that it effectively reintroduces compulsory student unionism. The speaker also criticised the fee as a tax on students, noted that 130,000 external students would pay without access to services, and said the guidelines give the minister sole control over spending.
